name: Grocery Outlet Holding Corp.

profile.description: Grocery Outlet Holding Corp., founded by Jim Read in 1946 and headquartered in Emeryville, California, is an extreme-value grocer that buys surplus and opportunistic name-brand products and sells them through stores run by independent operators [5]. FY2025 net sales were $4.69B with a GAAP net loss of $224.9M after impairments; Q2 2026 net sales rose 1.1% to $1.19B with comparable store sales down 0.3%, and the first half included a $158.0M goodwill impairment and $23.6M of restructuring charges tied to store closures [1][5]. CEO Jason Potter (ex-The Fresh Market) joined in February 2025 and is running a turnaround including a strategic review of UGO [2]. The stock trades at $12.93 (52-week range $5.66-$14.49), ~$1.28B market cap [5].

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Growth has come from extending the same opportunistic-buying, independent-operator model to new regions (revenue from $3.13B in 2020 to $4.69B in 2025), and the UGO acquisition is now under strategic review after store closures and impairments [5][2]. AI Deployment (1/2): The company promoted a VP of AI strategy and product solutions and says it is moving AI solutions 'from vision to measurable results', but no AI savings or products have been quantified [2]. Market Share (1/2): Grocery Outlet is a meaningful extreme-value grocer, but comparable store sales fell 1.0% in Q1 and 0.3% in Q2 2026, showing no share gains [1]. Product Pipeline (0/2): The pipeline is 30-33 net new stores for 2026, with no new formats or dated initiatives with revenue visibility [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): No R&D spend reported [5].

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): 'Touching Lives for the Better' is broad, but the model of delivering brand-name groceries at deep discounts through family-run independent operators gives it a clear customer and community purpose [4]. It is not articulated distinctively enough to score higher. Community Impact (1/2): The company's ESG reporting highlights diverting surplus food from waste and affordable food access in underserved areas, but no distinctive dollar-quantified giving program was found [4]. Employee Retention (0/2): No tenure or turnover data was found, and the company has had CEO turnover (RJ Sheedy departed in 2024, interim CEO, then Potter in 2025) [2]. Insider Buying (1/2): FMP insider statistics record 18 open-market purchases against 10 sales in Q1-Q3 2026, net buying during the turnaround, but dollar amounts for CEO-level purchases were not verified [5].

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored as a Growth stock (no dividend), 10 weight units. D/E of 226.7% (including lease liabilities) scores 0.32 [5]. TTM ROE of -40.1% (2x weight) and TTM net margin of -8.0% score 0, reflecting the Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 impairments [5][1]. Q2 2026 revenue growth of 1.1% scores 0.70, and the 2020-2025 revenue CAGR of 8.4% scores 0.89 at 2x weight [5]. Forward P/E of 19.4 (price $12.93 / FY2027 consensus EPS $0.666) scores 1.0, and FMP's forward PEG of 0.11 scores 1.0 at 2x weight; note consensus EPS growth of ~22% from FY2026 ($0.547) to FY2027 implies a PEG nearer 0.9, which would also score at or near 1.0 [5]. Weighted 5.81/10 rounds to 6. Liquidity is ample at ~2.5M shares/day (~$32M daily).

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): IMMUNE. Grocery Outlet sells physical food through physical stores, and its edge is human deal-making with CPG suppliers for surplus inventory plus local independent operators, none of which AI can substitute [1][2]. No analyst commentary flags AI as a risk; the company's challenges are consumer affordability pressure and expansion execution. AI could help with buying and pricing but is an efficiency tool here. AI Opportunity (0/1): No AI revenue [2].

infinite_game.summary: Grocery Outlet's 80-year-old independent-operator model is distinctive, but through Sinek's lens recent history is a finite-game story: rapid store expansion that securities suits now allege was unsustainable, CEO turnover, and a 2026 reset with store closures, a $158M goodwill impairment and a UGO strategic review [1][3]. CEO Jason Potter's decision to close unprofitable stores is a sign of courage, but there is no articulated Just Cause guiding strategy, and the core model has not reinvented itself.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): 'Touching Lives for the Better' and affordable brand-name food via family-run stores is a real purpose, but it is not framed as a vision of a better future that guides strategy; recent decisions have been driven by growth targets and then by profitability repair [4][2].

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Potter chose to close stores, take $158.0M of goodwill impairment and $23.6M of restructuring charges, and review UGO so that every market is profitable, accepting a 27.9% one-day share drop in March 2026 [1][2][3]. One costly corrective decision, not yet a pattern.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): The independent-operator model gives store owners real autonomy, but the corporate organization has gone through a CEO departure in 2024, an interim CEO, a new outside CEO in 2025, restructuring and multiple securities and derivative lawsuits over systems transition and expansion disclosures [2][3]. That is an unstable environment by Sinek's standard.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (0/2): The opportunistic-buying, independent-operator model has been unchanged since 1946; geographic expansion and the UGO acquisition were extensions, and the latter is now being reconsidered [2].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Management attributes comp weakness to affordability pressure on its core customer rather than framing Aldi, Lidl, dollar stores or Walmart as rivals that reveal weaknesses to learn from [2].

investment_thesis: Grocery Outlet's turnaround is showing early traction: Q2 2026 adjusted EPS of $0.20 beat the $0.12 consensus, and management raised FY2026 guidance to $4.70-4.72B net sales, comps of -0.5% to 0.0% and $0.51-0.55 adjusted EPS while still opening 30-33 net new stores [1]. At $12.93 the stock trades at ~0.27x sales and ~19x FY2027 consensus EPS of $0.67, with consensus expecting EPS to reach $0.74 in FY2028 [5]. The extreme-value grocery model is immune to AI substitution and benefits from trade-down demand, insiders were net buyers in 2026, and the Inspire Impact Score of 50 (ALIGNED) carries no negative attributions [5].
thesis_continued: The bear case is execution and balance sheet. Comparable store sales were negative in both reported 2026 quarters, Q3 guidance calls for comps of -1% to 0% including a ~100bp hit from a cyclospora food-safety issue, and GAAP results are deeply negative (TTM net margin -8.0%, ROE -40.1%) after a $158.0M goodwill impairment and restructuring [1][5]. D/E of ~227% including leases and negative TTM free cash flow limit flexibility, and the company faces consolidated securities class actions and derivative suits over its systems transition and an alleged unsustainable store-expansion strategy [3][5].
key_catalysts: Q3 2026 results against guidance of comps -1% to 0%, adjusted EBITDA $58-61M and adjusted EPS $0.14-0.16, a test of whether the turnaround holds through the cyclospora headwind [1]
Store-closure program and UGO strategic review aimed at making every market profitable, following $158.0M of goodwill impairment and $23.6M of restructuring in the first half of 2026 [1][2]
Consumer trade-down to extreme-value grocery as affordability pressure persists, with 30-33 net new stores planned for 2026 [1][2]
key_risks: Negative comparable store sales (Q1 -1.0%, Q2 -0.3%) and a ~100bp Q3 comp headwind from a cyclospora outbreak that could damage customer trust in fresh products [1]
Securities class actions (2025 systems-transition suit and 2026 suit alleging unsustainable store expansion) plus derivative suits create legal and governance overhang [3]
Leverage of ~227% D/E including leases and negative TTM free cash flow (capex exceeds operating cash flow) leave little room if the turnaround stalls [5]
